title: Light sources: things that make their own light

summary.text: Switch off a torch in a dark room, and the dark comes back at once. Some things make their own light: the Sun, a fire, a lamp, a torch, a phone screen, even a firefly. Scientists call them light sources. Other things, like a steel spoon or a mirror, only look bright when light falls on them. In a dark room, your child finds out which is which, and that a lamp gives light only while it is working.
summary.art: A girl in a dark room holding a lit torch, with a steel tumbler and a brass lamp beside her, and a sunny window drawn on the wall behind.

intro.hook: Switch off the lights in a room at night. Hold your hand in front of your face. Can you see it?
intro.text: In the dark, you cannot see your hand, even though it is right there. Now switch on a torch. Your hand is back! The torch made light, and the light let you see. In this unit you find out which things make their own light, and which things only look bright.
intro.art: A child in a dark room holding up one hand, and a torch beam just switched on, lighting up the hand.

outcomes: By the end I can say what a light source is: a thing that makes its own light.
By the end I can name light sources: the Sun, fire, lamps, torches, screens and fireflies.
By the end I can tell a light source from a shiny thing that only looks bright when light falls on it.
By the end I can show that a lamp or a torch gives light only while it is working, and say what it needs: oil, cells or electricity.
By the end I know the Sun is a star, and that I must never look straight at it.

terms.meaning: A light source is a thing that makes its own light.
terms.example: The Sun, a diya flame and a torch that is switched on are all light sources. A steel spoon is not.
terms.art: Four small pictures in a row: the Sun, a diya flame, a glowing torch and a phone screen, each with short rays around it.

terms.meaning: A flame is the bright, hot part of a fire. It makes light and heat.
terms.example: A diya has a small flame on its cotton wick.
terms.art: A clay diya with a yellow flame on the wick, a little blue at the bottom of the flame.

terms.meaning: A star is a huge ball of very hot gas that makes its own light. The Sun is a star.
terms.example: The Sun is the star nearest to us. The other stars are so far away that they look like tiny dots.
terms.art: A big bright Sun on one side, and a dark night sky full of tiny star dots on the other.

terms.meaning: A thing shines when light comes from it into our eyes. A light source shines with its own light. A shiny spoon shines only with light from somewhere else.
terms.example: A mirror shines in a sunny room, but not in a dark one.
terms.art: A shiny steel spoon in a sunny kitchen, bright, and the same spoon in a dark kitchen, nearly invisible.

explanations.concept: A light source makes its own light
explanations.definition: A light source is a thing that makes its own light. The Sun, fires, lamps, torches, screens, lightning and fireflies are light sources.
explanations.description: In the dark room test, you could see the torch only when it was switched on, and the phone only when its screen was on. These things make their own light, so you can see them even in the dark. Some light sources are made by nature, like the Sun and lightning. Some are made by people, like lamps and torches. Some are alive: a firefly makes light inside their body.
examples: In the dark room test, the torch shone the moment it was switched on.
A diya flame lights up a dark room in a power cut.
A firefly flashes their light to find other fireflies at night.
explanations.context: This card says what a light source is.
explanations.art: A dark room with three glowing things: a torch, a phone screen and a diya flame, and a firefly glowing outside the window.

explanations.concept: Shiny things only send back light
explanations.definition: A shiny thing, like a steel spoon or a mirror, makes no light of its own. It looks bright only when light from a light source falls on it.
explanations.description: In a bright room, the steel spoon and the mirror look very bright. Many children guess they make light. But in the dark room, you could not see them at all. When you pointed the torch at the spoon, it shone again. When you pointed the torch away, it vanished. The spoon was only sending back the torch's light.
examples: In the dark room test, the spoon vanished until the torch shone on it.
A steel tumbler shines next to a lamp, and goes dark when the lamp is taken away.
A mirror in a dark cupboard shows nothing.
explanations.context: This card is about shiny things that look bright but make no light.
explanations.art: Two pictures: a torch beam on a steel spoon, which shines, and the torch pointed away, with the spoon dark.

explanations.concept: A lamp makes light only while it is working
explanations.definition: A lamp or a torch does not keep light inside it. It makes new light every moment, as long as it has oil, cells or electricity.
explanations.description: When you switched the torch off, the dark came back at once. The torch had not kept any light inside. It makes new light only while it is switched on. A torch needs cells (people often call them batteries). A tube light needs electricity from the wires. A diya needs oil and a wick.
examples: In the dark room test, the dark came back the moment the torch was switched off.
In a power cut, every tube light goes dark at the same moment.
A diya goes out when all its oil is used up.
explanations.context: This card says why a lamp stops shining.
explanations.art: A torch drawn twice: switched on with a bright beam, and switched off with the room dark, and two cells beside it.

explanations.concept: The Sun is a star, and our biggest light source
explanations.definition: The Sun is a star: a huge ball of very hot gas that makes its own light. Almost all the light on Earth in the day comes from the Sun.
explanations.description: The Sun is so big that more than a million Earths could fit inside it. It is very far away, and its light takes about 8 minutes to reach us. The Sun never switches off. At night, our side of the Earth is turned away from it, so it is dark. Never look straight at the Sun, not even for a moment. Sunglasses and binoculars do not make it safe.
examples: Sunlight coming through a window lights up the whole room in the day.
Plants use sunlight to make their food.
On a cloudy day, the Sun is still shining above the clouds.
explanations.context: This card is about the Sun, the light source we need most.
explanations.art: A huge glowing Sun and the small round Earth far away, with one side of the Earth lit and the other side dark.

agreed.text: A light source makes its own light.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it in a dark room. A torch and a phone screen can be seen in the dark. A spoon, a mirror and a book cannot.

agreed.text: We see things that are not light sources only when light falls on them.
agreed.evidence: In the dark room, the spoon could be seen only while the torch was pointed at it.

agreed.text: The Sun is a star, made mostly of hydrogen gas.
agreed.evidence: In 1925, Cecilia Payne worked this out from the light of the Sun and other stars, using a rule made by the Indian scientist Meghnad Saha.

challenging.claim: Shiny things, like steel and mirrors, make their own light.
challenging.who: A common idea among young children, and many grown-ups
challenging.for: A steel tumbler or a mirror can look as bright as a lamp in a sunny room.
challenging.against: In a dark room, the tumbler and the mirror cannot be seen at all. They shine only when light from a source falls on them.
challenging.context: This card is about shiny things.

challenging.claim: The Sun stops shining at night.
challenging.who: A common idea among young children
challenging.for: At night we cannot see the Sun, and it is dark outside.
challenging.against: The Sun never stops shining. The Earth turns, and at night our side faces away from the Sun. At that moment, it is day on the other side of the Earth.
challenging.context: This card is about where the Sun goes at night.

big_questions.q: When you switched off the torch, the dark came back at once. Where did the light go?
big_questions.hint: The light flew out of the torch and landed on the walls, the floor and you. Things take in most of the light that lands on them.

big_questions.q: The steel spoon looked bright in the day. Why could you not see it in the dark?
big_questions.hint: Did the spoon have any light of its own? Where did its brightness come from in the day?

big_questions.q: Is a firefly a light source, like a torch? Are you a light source?
big_questions.hint: A firefly makes light inside their body. Your body gives off a tiny bit of light too, far too faint for eyes to see. Special cameras have photographed it.

big_questions.q: The oil in a diya came from sesame seeds or coconuts. Those plants grew in sunlight. Is a diya flame a little bit of old sunlight?
big_questions.hint: Plants use sunlight to make their food, and some of that food becomes oil.

big_questions.q: The Sun was shining long before there were any people. Was it making light, even with no eyes to see it?
big_questions.hint: Think of the torch shining in an empty room. Plants, animals and the sea all met the Sun's light before people did.

story.title: The Torch in the Power Cut
story.note: Power cuts at night are common in many Indian towns, and many families keep a torch and a lamp ready. Ammamma means grandmother in Malayalam and Telugu. Meenu, Kiran, Amma and Ammamma are made up.
text: Meenu was six. She lived in a flat on the third floor in Kochi, with her Amma, her grandmother Ammamma and her little brother Kiran.
One hot night, Meenu was colouring a parrot. Kiran was lining up his toy cars on the floor. The fan was whirring and the tube light was bright.
Then, click! The fan slowed down. The tube light went out. Everything went black.
"Ammamma!" shouted Kiran. "Where did the light go?"
"It is a power cut," said Ammamma calmly. "Stay where you are. I know where the torch is."
Meenu sat very still. She held her hand in front of her face. She could not see it at all. Out of the window, the whole street was dark too.
Then a small white circle appeared on the wall. Ammamma had found the torch. Now Meenu could see her crayons, Kiran's cars and Kiran's surprised face.
"The light came back!" said Kiran. "It was hiding in the torch."
Meenu was not so sure. "Was the light hiding in there all day, Ammamma?"
Ammamma smiled. "Let us find out. Watch the wall." She switched the torch off. Dark. She switched it on. Light. Off. Dark. On. Light.
Meenu thought hard. "If light was hiding in the torch, some would leak out when it is off," she said. "But it goes dark straight away."

"Yes," said Ammamma. "The torch has two cells inside. When I switch it on, they send electricity to a tiny lamp. The lamp makes new light every moment. When I switch it off, it stops making light. So the dark comes back at once."
Amma came in with the brass lamp and a box of matches. She lit the cotton wick. A yellow flame stood up, with a little blue at the bottom. The whole room glowed.
"The lamp makes light too!" said Kiran. He held up his steel tumbler. "And look, my tumbler is shining. My tumbler is a lamp!"
Meenu looked at the tumbler. It was bright on the side near the flame, and dark on the other side. "Let us test it," she said.
Amma carried the lamp into the kitchen. Ammamma switched off the torch. In the dark, Kiran held up his tumbler. Nobody could see it, not even Kiran.
"My tumbler stopped shining," said Kiran sadly.
"Your tumbler never made any light," said Meenu. "It was shining with the lamp's light. The lamp and the torch make their own light. Ammamma, what is that called?"
"A thing that makes its own light is called a light source," said Ammamma. "The torch is a light source. The lamp flame is a light source. The tumbler is not."
Kiran thought about it. "Is the Sun a light source?"
"The biggest one we have," said Ammamma. "The Sun is a star. It shines all the time, day and night. At night, our side of the Earth is turned away from it."
Amma came back with the lamp. Kiran held his tumbler near it again, and it shone. He moved it away, and it went dark. He laughed and did it again and again.
Just then, the fan began to whirr. The tube light flickered and came on. Everyone blinked.
"The light is back," said Kiran.
Meenu shook her head and smiled. "Not the same light, Kiran. The tube light is making brand-new light, right now. And now. And now."
Amma blew out the lamp, and the flame was gone in a blink. A thin line of smoke curled up from the wick.

Next morning, Meenu drew a picture. She drew the Sun, the brass lamp, the torch and the tube light, each with bright rays. In the corner she drew a steel tumbler, with no rays at all. Kiran coloured the tumbler silver, and drew the lamp right next to it.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Meenu finds that the torch and the lamp make new light every moment they are working, and the dark comes back the moment they stop. Kiran's steel tumbler shone only with the lamp's light and vanished in the dark, so looking bright is not the same as being a light source.
ask: When Ammamma switched the torch off, why did it go dark straight away?
Why could nobody see Kiran's tumbler in the dark?
Name three light sources in the story.
Meenu said the tube light was making brand-new light. What did she mean?
art: A flat at night with the tube light just gone out, a girl with a crayon and a small boy with toy cars, both looking up in the dark.
A grandmother holding a torch, making a white circle of light on the wall, and two children watching.
A mother lighting a brass lamp, and a small boy holding up a shining steel tumbler beside the flame.
A child's drawing of the Sun, a brass lamp, a torch and a tube light with rays, and a silver tumbler with no rays in the corner.

experiments.title: Light Maker or Not? The dark room test
experiments.context: In this experiment you gather some things from home and guess which ones make their own light. Then you take them into a dark room and find out.
experiments.question: Which of these things make their own light, and which only look bright?
experiments.predict: Look at each thing in the basket. Will you be able to see it in the dark room? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same dark room for every thing. We wait one whole minute in the dark before we start, so our eyes get used to it. We hold each thing in the same place, an arm's length in front of us.
results_table: My guess: will I see it in the dark?

materials.item: a torch that works (or a phone torch)
a phone or tablet whose screen can be switched on
a shiny steel spoon or steel tumbler
a small mirror
a shiny bangle, or a piece of kitchen foil
a sheet of white paper
a basket or a tray to carry it all

schedule.what: Guess which things will shine in the dark, then test each one in a dark room.

experiments.record: Draw two big circles. In one, draw the things you could see in the dark. In the other, draw the things that vanished. A grown-up writes the names.

setup.art: A tray in a bright room holding a torch, a phone, a steel spoon, a small mirror, a bangle and white paper.
setup.caption: 1. Put the things on a tray. Guess which will shine in the dark.

setup.art: A grown-up and a girl in a dark bathroom with the door shut, the girl holding up a steel spoon that cannot be seen.
setup.caption: 2. Go into a dark room. Wait one minute. Hold up each thing.

setup.art: The girl switching on a torch in the dark, its beam lighting up the steel spoon in her other hand.
setup.caption: 3. Switch the torch on and off. Shine it on the spoon.

flow.do: 1. In a bright room, put all the things on the tray. 2. Let your child hold and name each one. 3. Switch the torch and the phone screen on and off once.
flow.say: Here are some things from our home. Let's name them. Which ones look bright to you?
flow.kid: Hold each thing. Say its name. Which ones look bright?

flow.do: Ask your child to sort the things into two piles: 'will shine in the dark' and 'will vanish in the dark'. You write or draw their guesses in the table.
flow.say: Soon we will go into a dark room. Which things will you still be able to see there? Put them in this pile. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which things will you see in the dark? Make a pile. Why?

ask.q: Why did you put the spoon in that pile?
good: It is shiny, so it will shine.
It has no light of its own, so it will vanish.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Many children put the spoon, the mirror and the bangle in the 'will shine' pile, because they look so bright. Don't say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Take the tray into the darkest room you have, such as a bathroom with no window. 2. Close the door and switch off the light. 3. Wait one whole minute. 4. Ask your child to hold up a hand.
flow.say: Let's wait for one minute, so our eyes get used to the dark. Now hold up your hand. Can you see it?
flow.kid: Wait in the dark. Count to sixty with me. Can you see your hand?
flow.parent: Do this after dark if you can. If some light comes under the door, put a towel along the gap. A little light is fine: things will look dim instead of vanishing, and you can still compare them.

flow.do: 1. Hand your child the spoon, the mirror, the bangle, the paper and the switched-off torch, one at a time. 2. Each time, ask if they can see it. 3. Then ask them to switch the phone screen on.
flow.say: Hold up the spoon. Can you see it? Now the mirror. Now the bangle. Now the torch, switched off. Now switch on the phone screen. What happens?
flow.kid: Hold up each thing. Can you see it? Now switch on the phone.

good: Only the phone, when its screen was on.
I could not see the spoon or the mirror.

flow.do: 1. Your child switches the torch on and points it at the ceiling. 2. Then off, and on again, three times. 3. Then they shine it on the spoon, and then point it away from the spoon.
flow.say: Switch the torch on. Now off. Is any light left? Now shine it on the spoon. Now point it away. What happens to the spoon?
flow.kid: Switch the torch on and off. Shine it on the spoon. Now point it away.

ask.q: What happened when you switched the torch off?
good: It went dark straight away.
No light was left.
It shone when the torch was on it.
It went dark when I pointed the torch away.

flow.parent: Look for two things. The dark comes back the instant the torch goes off. And the spoon shines only while the torch beam is on it.

flow.do: Back in the bright room, look at the guesses together. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Which things shone in the dark? Which vanished? Were your guesses right? Why do you think the spoon vanished?
flow.kid: Which things shone in the dark? Which vanished? Why?

good: Only the torch and the phone shone in the dark.
The spoon only shines when light is on it.
The torch made light only while it was on.

check.q: Lakshmi is in a dark room with a steel spoon and a torch that is switched on. Which one makes its own light?
check.why: The torch is a light source: it makes its own light. The spoon makes no light. Lakshmi can see the spoon only when the torch shines on it.

experiments.title: Which Light Shows the Far Wall?
experiments.context: In this experiment you stand at one end of a dark room with three different light sources. You find out which one lets you see a drawing on the far wall.
experiments.question: Do all light sources give the same amount of light?
experiments.predict: Which will help you see the drawing best: the phone screen or the torch? Why do you think so? (If you do the diya extra, guess for the diya too.)
experiments.fair_test: We stand in the same place each time, and hold each light at the same height. We use one light at a time. We look at the same drawing every time.
results_table: Light source (phone, torch, and diya if you use it)
My guess: can I see the drawing?

materials.item: a drawing with bright colours, such as a big red flower and a blue bird, stuck on a wall
a torch
a phone with its screen switched on, but its torch off
extra, only if a grown-up is happy to light it: a diya or a candle on a steel plate, and a matchbox (for a grown-up only)

experiments.safety: If you do the diya extra, only a grown-up lights, carries and blows out the diya or candle. Keep it on a steel plate, away from curtains and clothes.

schedule.what: Light a far drawing with a phone screen, a torch and a diya, one at a time.

experiments.record: Draw the three lights in a row. Next to each one, draw what you could see of the drawing on the wall.

setup.art: A colourful drawing of a red flower and a blue bird stuck on a wall, at the far end of a dark room.
setup.caption: 1. Stick a bright drawing on the far wall.

setup.art: A girl at the other end of the dark room, holding a phone screen towards the wall, the drawing very dim.
setup.caption: 2. Hold up one light at a time. Look at the drawing.

setup.art: The same girl shining a torch at the drawing, its colours now bright and clear.
setup.caption: 3. Which light shows the colours best?

flow.do: 1. Stick the drawing on a wall at the far end of a room. 2. Mark a spot to stand at the other end, about four big steps away.
flow.say: Here is a drawing of a flower and a bird. Soon it will be dark. Which light will help you see it from over here?
flow.kid: Look at the drawing. Soon it will be dark.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess which light will show the drawing best, and which worst. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: Phone screen or torch: which will show the drawing best? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which light will show the drawing best? Why?

good: The torch, because it is the brightest.
The diya, because fire is strong.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Don't say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Switch off the room light and wait one minute. 2. Your child holds up the phone screen, facing the drawing. 3. Then the torch, pointed at the drawing. 4. Extra, if a grown-up is happy to light a flame: you hold up the lit diya at the same spot.
flow.say: First the phone screen. Can you see the drawing? Can you see its colours? Now the torch. (Extra: now the diya.)
flow.kid: Hold up the phone. Can you see the drawing? Now try the torch.

ask.q: Which light showed the colours best?
good: The torch. I could see the red and the blue.
With the phone, it was too dark.

flow.parent: The torch usually shows the drawing clearly. The phone screen and the diya make much less light, so the drawing looks dim and its colours are hard to see. A bright phone torch works like a torch.

flow.do: Switch on the room light. Compare what happened with the guesses. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Which light made the most light? Were your guesses right? Do all light sources give the same amount of light?
flow.kid: Which light was brightest? Do all lights give the same light?

good: Some light sources make more light than others.
The torch was brightest.

check.q: Revathi has a phone screen and a torch in a dark room. She wants to see a toy far away. Which should she use?
options: Either: they give the same light
check.why: Both are light sources, but a torch makes much more light than a phone screen and sends it forward in a beam. So the torch lights the far toy best.

activities.title: Follow the Light Home
activities.context: In this activity you find bright patches in your home in the day, and follow each one back to where its light comes from.

materials.item: nothing to buy: a room with a window, in the day

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun, not even through a window.

schedule.what: Find bright patches at home and follow each one back to its light source.

activities.record: Draw one bright patch in your home, and draw a line back to its light source.

setup.art: A bright patch of sunlight on a tiled floor, and a girl pointing from the patch to the window.
setup.caption: 1. Find a bright patch. Point to where the light comes from.

setup.art: The girl pointing from a bright spot on a table up to a lit lamp on the ceiling.
setup.caption: 2. Find another. Is it the Sun, a lamp, or something else?

flow.do: Walk round the home with your child. Find a bright patch on the floor, a wall or a table.
flow.say: Look, this bit of the floor is bright. Where is its light coming from? Point to it.
flow.kid: Find a bright patch. Where does its light come from? Point.

flow.do: 1. Find three or four bright patches. 2. For each, your child points back to the light source: the window, a lamp, a screen. 3. If a patch comes from a mirror or a steel plate, ask where that light came from first.
flow.say: This one comes from the window. And the light at the window comes from the Sun. What about this shiny patch from the steel plate?
flow.kid: Find more bright patches. Follow each one back. Where does it start?

ask.q: Where did the light on the steel plate come from?
good: From the window first.
From the Sun, and then the plate sent it on.

flow.parent: Children love finding that a bright spot from a mirror or a steel plate leads back to the window. The light starts at a light source every time.

flow.do: Ask how many patches started at the Sun, and how many at a lamp.
flow.say: How many bright patches did the Sun make? How many did the lamps make? Which light source lit most of our home today?
flow.kid: Which light made most bright patches today? The Sun or a lamp?

ask.q: Which light source lit most of the home?
good: The Sun, through the windows.
In the day, mostly the Sun.

activities.title: The Little Lights Hunt at night
activities.context: In this activity you switch off the big lights at night and hunt for every tiny light that is still on in your home.

materials.item: nothing to buy: your home at night, with the big lights off
paper and a pencil, for tally marks

schedule.what: Switch off the big lights and count the small light sources still on.

activities.record: Make one tally mark for each little light you find. Draw your favourite one.

setup.art: A dark living room at night with tiny glowing dots: a red dot on a TV, a green dot on a phone charger, and a glowing clock.
setup.caption: 1. Switch off the big lights. Look for tiny lights.

setup.art: A girl and a grown-up in the dark, the girl making a tally mark on paper by the glow of a charger light.
setup.caption: 2. Make a tally mark for each one.

flow.do: After dark, switch off the fans and big lights in one or two rooms. Wait one minute together.
flow.say: The big lights are off. Some tiny lights are still on. How many do you think we will find? Why?
flow.kid: The big lights are off. How many tiny lights will we find? Why?

flow.do: 1. Walk slowly round with your child. 2. Look for tiny lights: on the TV, a charger, a clock or the inverter. 3. Open the fridge, and look out of the window too. 4. Make a tally mark for each one.
flow.say: Look! A little red light on the TV. That is a light source. Make a mark. Can you find another one?
flow.kid: Find a tiny light. Make a mark. Find another.
flow.parent: Most homes have more tiny lights than children expect. Don't touch switches or plugs. Just look.

flow.do: Count the marks together. Ask what all the little lights need to keep shining.
flow.say: How many did we find? Was that more or fewer than you guessed? What do these lights need to keep shining?
flow.kid: How many did you find? What do they need to keep shining?

good: Electricity.
If the power goes, they go out.

activities.title: The Diya Up Close
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up lights a diya, and you look closely at the flame from a safe distance.

materials.item: a clay or brass diya with oil and a cotton wick, on a steel plate
a matchbox (for a grown-up only)

activities.safety: Only a grown-up lights and blows out the diya. Sit an arm's length away. Never put your hand above the flame: the hot air rises straight up. Tie back long hair and keep dupattas away.

schedule.what: Watch a diya flame closely, from a safe distance.

activities.record: Draw the diya and its flame. Colour the parts of the flame you saw.

setup.art: A grown-up lighting a clay diya on a steel plate, and a boy sitting an arm's length away.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up lights the diya. Sit an arm's length away.

setup.art: A close-up of a diya flame: blue at the bottom, bright yellow above, with the dark wick in the middle.
setup.caption: 2. Look at the colours of the flame.

flow.do: Light the diya on its steel plate. Sit your child an arm's length away.
flow.say: I am lighting the diya. Sit here, an arm's length away. What do you see?
flow.kid: Sit an arm's length away. Watch the grown-up light the diya.

flow.do: Ask your child to look at the flame's shape and colours, and at the wick.
flow.say: What shape is the flame? What colours can you see? Look at the bottom of the flame. Look at the wick.
flow.kid: What shape is the flame? What colours do you see?

good: Yellow on top.
A little blue at the bottom.
The wick is black.

flow.parent: A diya flame is mostly yellow, with a small blue part at the bottom. The yellow light comes from tiny bits of soot that glow because they are so hot.

flow.do: Hold the back of your own hand beside the flame, a hand's width away, never above it. Let your child do the same if they are careful.
flow.say: Put the back of your hand beside the flame, not above it. Not too close. What do you feel?
flow.kid: Hold your hand beside the flame, not above. What do you feel?

good: It is warm.
The flame makes heat as well as light.

flow.do: Ask what the flame needs to keep burning. Then blow it out.
flow.say: What does the diya need to keep making light? What will happen when all the oil is gone? Now I will blow it out.
flow.kid: What does the diya need to keep shining? Watch it go out.

good: Oil.
A wick.
Air.

check.q: Ramya's diya has burnt for a long time. Now its oil is all used up. What will happen?
check.why: A diya makes light only while it has oil to burn. When the oil is gone, the flame goes out.

games.title: Yellow Paper, Dark Paper: a card sorting game
games.players: 1 to 4 players, and a grown-up to read the cards (the grown-up can play too).
games.context: This is a card game. You sort cards onto three papers: things that make their own light, things that don't, and things that could but aren't right now.

items.b: LIGHT SOURCE. The Sun is a star. It makes its own light.
LIGHT SOURCE. The flame makes light as it burns oil.

img.credit: siddarth varanasi, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.b: LIGHT SOURCE. It makes light while its cells send electricity.
NOT NOW. A switched-off torch makes no light.
LIGHT SOURCE. It makes light while electricity flows.
LIGHT SOURCE. A firefly makes their own light inside their body.

img.credit: Teja Yantrapalli, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.b: LIGHT SOURCE. Lightning is a giant spark that makes light.
LIGHT SOURCE. The screen makes its own light.
LIGHT SOURCE. Burning wood makes light and heat.
NOT A LIGHT SOURCE. It only shines when light falls on it.
NOT A LIGHT SOURCE. It only sends back light from somewhere else.
NOT A LIGHT SOURCE. In the dark, you cannot see it.

items.f: A white page of a book
items.b: NOT A LIGHT SOURCE. You need a light to read it.
NOT NOW. It will make light only when it is lit.
NOT A LIGHT SOURCE. Light can pass through it, but it makes none.

items.f: A star in the night sky
items.b: LIGHT SOURCE. Every star makes its own light, like our Sun.

rules: Mix the 16 cards and put them in a pile, face down.
Lay three papers on the floor: a yellow paper for LIGHT SOURCE, a dark paper for NOT A LIGHT SOURCE, and a white paper for NOT NOW (a thing that could make light but is not making it right now).
Take turns, the youngest first. On your turn, take the top card. A grown-up reads the front out loud.
Put the card on the paper you think is right, and say why.
The grown-up turns the card over and reads the back. If you were right, leave the card face up on its paper. If you were wrong, move it to the right paper and turn it face down.
When all 16 cards are sorted, count the cards that are face up. The team wins if 12 or more of the 16 are face up. Play again to beat your score.
Look at the cards on the NOT NOW paper. For each one, ask: what would make this one a light source?

setup.art: Sixteen cards in a pile on the floor, and a yellow paper, a dark paper and a white paper laid side by side.
setup.caption: 1. Put out a yellow, a dark and a white paper.

setup.art: A girl putting the card 'A steel spoon' on the dark paper, and a grown-up turning over a card to read the back.
setup.caption: 2. Sort each card. Turn it over to check.

flow.do: Lay out the yellow, dark and white papers. Read the rules together.
flow.say: Yellow is for things that make their own light. Dark is for things that don't. White is for things that could, but are not making light right now. Let's sort the cards.
flow.kid: Yellow: makes light. Dark: makes no light. White: not now. Let's sort.

flow.do: Play through all 16 cards, taking turns. Read each card's front, wait for the player's choice and reason, then read the back.
flow.say: A shiny gold bangle. Yellow, dark or white? Why? Let's turn it over and see.
flow.kid: Read the card. Yellow, dark or white? Why? Turn it over.
flow.parent: The shiny cards (the spoon, the mirror and the bangle) are the tricky ones. Remind your child of the dark room test if they have done it.

flow.do: Count the face-up cards. Then look at the cards on the white NOT NOW paper and ask what would make each one a light source.
flow.say: The torch is switched off, and the candle is not lit. What would make them light sources?
flow.kid: What would make the torch and the candle shine?

check.q: Nisha, a girl in your class, says a mirror is a light source because it shines. Is she right?
options: No, a mirror only sends back light from somewhere else
Yes, a mirror makes its own light
check.why: A mirror makes no light of its own. In a dark room you cannot see it. It shines only when light from a light source falls on it.

games.title: Torch On, Torch Off: a moving game
games.players: 2 or more players. One player is the caller.
games.context: This is a moving game. The caller reads a card, and everyone shows with their hands and body what the light does.

items.f: Torch on! Open both hands wide.
items.b: Light is coming out.

items.f: Torch off! Close both hands into fists.
items.b: The light stops at once.

items.f: The diya is lit! Wave your fingers up like a flame.
items.b: A diya flame makes light while it burns.

items.f: Blow out the diya! Blow, then make fists.
items.b: The light is gone.

items.f: The Sun rises! Stand tall and make a big circle with your arms.
items.b: The Sun is a star and makes its own light.
The Sun still shines on the other side of the Earth.

items.f: A firefly flashes! Open and close one hand, quick as a blink.
items.b: A firefly makes light inside their body.

items.f: Power cut! Freeze with your fists closed.
items.b: Every tube light goes dark.

items.f: The power is back! Open your hands wide.
items.b: The tube lights make new light again.
A spoon makes no light. It waits for a light to shine on it.

rules: Mix the 10 caller cards. The caller holds them.
The caller reads the front of a card out loud. A grown-up reads for a caller who cannot read yet.
The caller and everyone else do the move on the front as fast as they can.
The caller asks: why? A player who can say why the light does that gets one point.
The caller reads the back, so everyone knows the answer.
After Night time, turn round to face the caller again before the next card.
After all 10 cards, the player with the most points wins. If only one child plays, try to get 7 points or more out of 10. Swap callers and play again if you like.

setup.art: A girl holding up a card that says Torch off, and two children closing their hands into fists.
setup.caption: 1. The caller reads a card.

setup.art: Two children making big circles with their arms, as the caller holds up a card that says The Sun rises.
setup.caption: 2. Everyone does the move.

flow.do: Practise the moves for 'Torch on' and 'Torch off' together.
flow.say: Torch on: open your hands wide, light is coming out. Torch off: fists, quick! The light stops at once.
flow.kid: Torch on: hands wide open. Torch off: fists, fast!

flow.do: Play all 10 cards. After each move, ask 'why?' before you read the back. After 'Night time', ask where the Sun is.
flow.say: Night time! Turn your back. Is the Sun still shining? Where?
flow.kid: Do each move. Is the Sun still shining at night?

ask.q: Where is the Sun at night?
good: Still shining, on the other side of the Earth.
Our side has turned away from it.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: When the power comes back, what do the tube lights have to do? What do they need?
flow.kid: The power is back! What do tube lights need to shine?

check.q: Faiz plays 'Power cut!'. The tube light goes dark. What does it need to shine again?
check.why: A tube light makes light only while electricity reaches it. When the power comes back, it makes new light.

projects.title: The Paper-Cup Star Lantern
projects.context: In this project you make a lantern from a paper cup with holes in its bottom. On the second night you put it over a torch, and fill the ceiling with spots of light.

materials.item: a paper cup that fits over the lit end of your torch
a pencil with a sharp point, or a compass point (for a grown-up)
a ball of atta dough or modelling clay, to hold inside the cup
crayons or sketch pens
a torch

projects.safety: A grown-up makes the holes. Push the point down into the dough inside the cup, away from fingers.

schedule.what: Draw dots on the cup, then a grown-up pokes a hole through each dot.
At night, hold the cup over a torch and look at the spots of light.

projects.record: Draw your cup, and draw the spots of light it made on the ceiling.

setup.art: A paper cup upside down with crayon dots drawn on its flat bottom, a ball of dough inside it, and a grown-up poking a pencil through a dot.
setup.caption: 1. Draw dots. A grown-up pokes a hole through each one.

setup.art: A dark bedroom with a girl holding a torch pointing up, the cup over its lit end, and spots of light all over the ceiling.
setup.caption: 2. At night, hold the cup over a torch.

flow.do: Your child draws 6 to 10 dots on the flat bottom of the cup, keeping them apart. They can make a shape, like a star or a fish.
flow.say: Draw dots on the bottom of the cup. Each dot will become a hole. What shape will you make?
flow.kid: Draw dots on the cup's bottom. You can make a shape.

flow.do: 1. Press the ball of dough inside the cup, up under the flat bottom. 2. Hold the cup upside down on the table. 3. Push the pencil point through each dot into the dough. 4. Your child counts the holes.
flow.say: I will make a hole through each dot. Let's count them. How many spots of light do you think we will see?
flow.kid: Count the holes. How many spots of light will you see?

flow.do: 1. On the next night, switch off the lights. 2. Hold the torch switched on, pointing up. 3. Put the cup over its lit end, like a hat. 4. Slowly lift the torch and cup towards the ceiling, and back down.
flow.say: Look up! What do you see? How many spots? Where does each spot's light come from?
flow.kid: Look up at the ceiling. Count the spots. Where does the light come from?

ask.q: Where does the light come from?
good: From the torch, through the holes.
The cup makes no light. The torch does.

flow.parent: Each hole lets a little torch light out, so each one makes one spot. Lifting the torch and cup makes the spots bigger and dimmer. If the cup is too small, hold the torch's lit end just under it.

flow.do: Switch the torch off and on. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Switch the torch off. What happens to the spots? Why?
flow.kid: Switch the torch off. Where did the spots go?

check.q: Anjali switches off the torch under her star lantern. What happens to the spots on the ceiling?
options: They turn into one big spot
check.why: The spots are torch light coming through the holes. With the torch off, no light is made, so all the spots vanish at once.

challenges.title: Read in the Power Cut
challenges.context: This is a problem to solve. Pretend there is a power cut at night. You want to look at a picture book. How can you light it up?
challenges.problem: Gayatri and a grown-up want to read a picture book together, but the power has gone. How can they light up the page well enough to see the pictures?
constraints: Pretend the room lights and fans do not work.
Only a grown-up may use a flame.
Use only things you already have at home.
general: Many families keep a torch or an emergency lamp ready for power cuts.
People light a diya or a candle, and keep it on a plate.
Some homes have solar lamps, which store sunlight's energy in the day and give light at night.
creative: Stand a torch so it points at the ceiling. The white ceiling spreads the light around the room.
Hold a white paper or a steel plate beside the book, to send more of the torch's light onto the page.
Shine the torch at a mirror, and turn the mirror so the light lands on the book.
challenges.your_turn: Find two ways to light the book. Which way let you see the colours best? Which light source did each way start with?

setup.art: A grown-up and a girl in a dark room with a picture book, a torch, a phone, a steel plate and a mirror on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Pretend the power has gone. How will you light the book?

setup.art: The girl shining a torch at the white ceiling, and soft light falling on the book in the grown-up's lap.
setup.caption: 2. Try your ideas. Which works best?

flow.do: Switch off the lights. Read the problem to your child.
flow.say: Pretend it is a power cut. We want to read this book. What could we use to light it up?
flow.kid: It is a pretend power cut. How can you light up the book?

good: The torch.
The phone.
The mirror, with the torch.

flow.do: Let your child try their ideas. Help only if asked. If they try the mirror or the plate alone, ask why it does not work.
flow.say: Try your idea. Can you see the pictures? Can you see the colours? Does the mirror work without the torch?
flow.kid: Try your idea. Can you see the pictures? Try another way.
flow.parent: A mirror or a steel plate on its own makes no light. With a torch, it can send light onto the page. Every way that works starts with a light source.

flow.do: Ask which way worked best, and why. Then the check question.
flow.say: Which way was best? Which light source did it start with?
flow.kid: Which way was best? Which light did it start with?

check.q: Gayatri holds a steel plate next to her book in the dark. No torch is on. Will the plate light up the book?
options: No, the plate makes no light
Only if she holds it close
check.why: A steel plate is not a light source. It can only send back light that falls on it. In the dark, with no torch, it has no light to send.

items.p: A grown-up reads each one. Is it a light source? Colour the light sources yellow. Leave the others white.
items.why: A light source makes its own light. The Sun, the lit candle and the switched-on torch do. The tumbler, the mirror and the book only look bright when light falls on them.

items.p: Draw a line from each light source to what it needs to keep shining.
items.why: Every lamp needs something to keep making light. A diya burns oil. A torch uses its cells. A tube light uses electricity from the wires.
items.art: A diya, a torch and a tube light on the left. A bottle of oil, two torch cells and a wall switch on the right.

items.p: Draw three light sources you can find in your home. Draw rays coming out of each one.
items.a: Three light sources, such as a tube light, a torch, a phone screen, a diya or the Sun through a window, each with rays.
items.why: A strong drawing shows things that make their own light, not shiny things like steel or mirrors.
items.art: Three empty boxes, each with a small sun-ray shape in the corner.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why could you not see the steel spoon in the dark room?
items.a: The spoon makes no light of its own. It shines only when light falls on it, and in the dark there was no light.
items.why: A strong answer says the spoon is not a light source, and that it needs light from somewhere else to shine.

items.p: The power has gone at night. Three people in one home have different ideas about which light to use.

views.says: Light the diya. It needs no cells and no charging. We always have oil in the kitchen.
Use the torch. It has no flame, so nothing can catch fire. It is brighter too.
Use the phone. It is already in my hand.

items.ask: Which light would you choose? Why? Then say one good thing about someone else's idea.
items.a: Any choice with a good reason. The diya needs no electricity but has a flame. The torch is bright and safe but its cells run out. The phone is handy but its screen is dim and uses up its charge.
items.why: A strong answer gives a real reason for its choice, and fairly says what is good about another choice. Each light source needs something different to keep shining.

items.p: Look at this room at night. A grown-up points to each thing. Say 'light source' or 'not a light source', and the grown-up writes it.
items.why: The tube light and the phone screen make their own light. The steel plate and the window glass make none: they only look bright when light falls on them or passes through.
items.art: A room at night with a glowing tube light, a steel plate on a table, a phone screen glowing on a bed and a dark window, each with an empty label.

items.p: Look at the street at night. Count the light sources. Write the number.
items.why: There are 5 light sources: two street lights, a lamp over a shop door, a scooter's headlight and a star. The scooter's mirror and the steel gate are not light sources, because they only shine with light from somewhere else.
items.art: A street at night with two street lights, a lit lamp over a shop door, a scooter with its headlight on, one star in the sky, a shiny scooter mirror and a steel gate.

items.p: The Sun is a star, and it is a light source.
items.why: True. The Sun is a huge ball of very hot gas that makes its own light. It is the star nearest to us.

items.p: In the story, Kiran says his steel tumbler is a lamp. What is the best way to test it?
opts: Take it into a dark room and see if it still shines
Look at it in a sunny room
items.why: A light source can be seen in the dark. Kiran's tumbler vanished in the dark, so it makes no light of its own.

items.p: Which of these gives heat as well as light?
items.why: A flame makes heat and light. The spoon and the mirror make neither.

items.p: Put these in order, 1 to 4: what happened in the dark room?
items: I could see the spoon in the beam.
I switched off the torch, and it was dark again.
items.why: The room starts dark. The torch makes light, and the spoon shines when the beam falls on it. When the torch is off, no light is made, and the dark comes back.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: your torch is getting dimmer and dimmer. What could be wrong? What would you do?
items.a: The cells are running out. I would put new cells in, or charge it.
items.why: A strong answer says a torch needs energy from its cells to make light, so dim light means the cells are running out.

items.p: In the dark room, you shine the torch on the steel spoon. Draw what you see. Draw the light going from the torch to the spoon.
items.a: A torch with a beam, and a spoon shining where the beam lands. The rest is dark.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the light starting at the torch and landing on the spoon. The spoon shines only where the torch light falls.

items.p: It is Karthigai Deepam. Two friends talk about how to light up their balcony.

views.says: We should light clay diyas. The oil comes from plants, and the flames are beautiful. Our families have always done it.
We should use LED lights. There is no flame and no smoke, so nothing can catch fire. They use very little electricity.

items.ask: Which would you choose? Why? Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: Either choice, with a good reason. Diyas need no electricity and use oil from plants, but they have flames and make smoke. LED lights are safe and use little electricity, but they need power from the wires.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason, and fairly names something good about the other choice. Both are real light sources. Each needs something different to keep shining.

items.p: Which light source do we never need to switch on or fill up?
items.why: The Sun makes its own light all the time. Nobody needs to switch it on, fill it with oil or put cells in it.

items.p: Draw a line from each light source to where you would find it.
pairs: By the sea, to guide ships
items.why: Light sources are found in many places. Some are made by people, like lighthouses and street lights. Some are made by nature, like lightning, and some are living beings, like fireflies.
items.art: A lighthouse, a street light, a firefly and a lightning bolt on the left. The sea, a road, trees at night and a storm cloud on the right.

items.p: Label the parts of this diya. A grown-up reads the words: flame, wick, oil, clay pot.
items.why: The flame makes the light. The wick carries oil up to the flame. The oil is what burns. The clay pot holds the oil.
items.art: A clay diya drawn large, with a flame, a cotton wick, a pool of oil inside, and four empty labels with lines.

items.p: Rani, a girl in Class 1, says: 'In a power cut, the light runs away to the power station.' Say what you would tell her, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: The light does not run away. The tube light stops making light because no electricity comes to it. When the power comes back, it makes new light.
items.why: A strong answer says a lamp makes light only while electricity reaches it. The light is not stored anywhere waiting to come back.

items.p: A solar lamp is put in the sun all day. When can it give light?
opts: At night, using the energy it stored in the day
Only while the sun shines on it
items.why: A solar lamp stores energy from sunlight in the day, and uses it to make light at night.

items.p: Two torches are the same, but one has weak cells and one has fresh cells. Which one lights the far wall better?
items.why: A torch makes light from the energy in its cells. Weak cells give less light, so the far wall looks dim.

opts: A thing that makes its own light
A thing you can see through
quiz.why: A light source makes its own light, like the Sun or a lit diya. A shiny thing that only looks bright is not a light source.

quiz.p: Which of these is a light source?
quiz.why: A lit candle makes its own light. The steel plate and the mirror only shine with light from somewhere else.
A firefly is a living being who makes their own light inside their body.

quiz.p: Why does a mirror look bright in a sunny room?
quiz.why: A mirror makes no light. It looks bright because sunlight falls on it and bounces off into our eyes.

quiz.p: Kavitha switches off the tube light at night. Why does the room go dark?
opts: The tube light stops making light
The light goes back into the tube
The light runs out of the window
quiz.why: A tube light makes new light only while electricity flows through it. Switch it off, and it stops making light.

quiz.p: What does a torch need to make light?
quiz.why: A torch uses the electricity from its cells. When the cells run out, the torch stops shining.

opts: A big lamp in the sky
quiz.why: The Sun is a star: a huge ball of very hot gas that makes its own light. It is the nearest star to us.

quiz.p: Pooja wants to see the Sun better. What should she do?
opts: Look at it for just one second
quiz.why: The Sun is so bright it can harm your eyes, even in one second and even through sunglasses. Never look straight at the Sun.

quiz.p: Where is the Sun at night?
opts: Still shining, on the other side of the Earth
quiz.why: The Sun never stops shining. At night, our side of the Earth is turned away from it.

quiz.p: Which of these is a light source made by nature?
quiz.why: Lightning is a giant spark in the sky that makes light. A tube light and a torch are made by people.

applications: Lighthouses, like the one on Marina Beach in Chennai, shine a bright light at night so that ships can find the coast.
Street lights and the headlights of buses and scooters let people see the road at night.
Families keep torches, lamps and diyas ready for power cuts.
Solar lamps store energy from sunlight in the day, and give light at night in homes without electricity.
Most white LED lights use a blue LED with a yellow coating. Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura in Japan made the first bright blue LEDs. They won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2014.

spotted.text: At Karthigai Deepam in Tamil Nadu, homes are lit with rows of clay diyas, and a huge flame is lit on the hill at Tiruvannamalai.
spotted.art: A doorstep with a kolam and a row of small lit clay diyas, and a far hill with a big flame on top.

spotted.text: In many homes in Kerala, a tall brass lamp called a nilavilakku is lit in the evening.
spotted.art: A tall brass nilavilakku with several small flames, in a Kerala home with a wooden door.

spotted.text: On Sundays and festival nights, Mysuru Palace is lit up with nearly a hundred thousand bulbs.
spotted.art: A big palace at night outlined with thousands of tiny yellow bulbs.

spotted.text: The lighthouse on Marina Beach in Chennai flashes its light out over the sea every night.
spotted.art: A tall lighthouse by a beach at night, with a beam of light sweeping out over the waves.

spotted.text: Before the monsoon, in villages near Bhandardara in Maharashtra, trees twinkle with thousands of fireflies.
spotted.art: Dark trees at night covered in tiny green-yellow flashing dots of firefly light.

spotted.text: In Chandannagar in West Bengal, lighting artists make huge pictures out of tiny lights for Jagaddhatri Puja.
spotted.art: A street at night with a giant peacock made of thousands of tiny coloured lights.

spotted.text: At Dev Deepawali in Varanasi, the steps along the Ganga are covered with lit diyas.
spotted.art: Long riverside steps at night covered with rows of tiny diya flames, reflected in the water.

open_questions.q: How long does light take to get out from the middle of the Sun?
open_questions.why_open: Light made deep inside the Sun bumps into the gas again and again on its way out. Scientists think this takes many thousands of years, but their answers differ by a lot.

open_questions.q: How do thousands of fireflies on one tree flash together?
open_questions.why_open: In some places, such as parts of Southeast Asia, whole trees of fireflies flash at the same time. Scientists know each firefly watches the others' flashes, but they are still studying how so many keep time together.

open_questions.q: How did living beings first learn to make light?
open_questions.why_open: Many kinds of living beings make light: fireflies, some fish, some mushrooms and tiny sea creatures. Scientists think living light began separately many times, but nobody knows exactly how it started.

ask_kids: How many light sources can you see right now?
Is the light in the kitchen a light source? What about the steel vessels?
What would happen to the plants if the Sun stopped shining?
Which light source do you like best? Why?
Is a fire in a kitchen stove a light source too?

jokes.j: Why did the torch go to school?
What did the spoon say in the dark cupboard?
Why was the Sun never late for school?
jokes.a: It always got up at sunrise!

jokes.j: What did the diya say when the oil ran out?
Why did the firefly get good marks?
What did the torch say to the cells?
Why did the mirror feel shy in the dark?
What do you call a lamp that tells jokes?

maths.problem: In the dark room test, Meena, a girl in Class 1, guessed that 5 things would shine. Only 2 really did: the torch and the phone. How many fewer shone than she guessed?
maths.explain: Count on from 2 to 5: 3, 4, 5. That is 3. So 3 fewer things shone than Meena guessed. The others were shiny things.
maths.context: This is about the dark room test, where you found which things shine in the dark.
maths.why_maths: Taking away shows how many of the guesses were wrong, and those are the things worth thinking about.

maths.problem: On the Little Lights Hunt, Sowmya found 3 tiny lights in the kitchen and 4 in the hall. Which room had more? How many did she find in all?
maths.explain: 4 is more than 3, so the hall had more. 3 and 4 make 7, so Sowmya found 7 little lights in all.
maths.context: This is about the Little Lights Hunt, where you counted tiny lights at night.
maths.why_maths: Tally marks help us count every light, and comparing the counts shows where the most light sources are.

maths.problem: Joseph's star lantern has 6 holes, and it makes 6 spots on the ceiling. He pokes 4 more holes. How many spots will he see now?
maths.explain: Each hole lets out a little torch light and makes one spot. 6 holes and 4 more holes make 10 holes. So he will see 10 spots.
maths.context: This is about the Paper-Cup Star Lantern, where a torch makes spots on the ceiling.
maths.why_maths: Knowing that one hole makes one spot lets us predict the spots before we switch on the torch.

maths.problem: For Karthigai Deepam, Anu sets lamps in a row: diya, diya, LED, diya, diya, LED, diya, diya. What comes next?
maths.explain: The pattern is two diyas, then one LED, again and again. After two diyas comes an LED.
maths.context: This is about lighting lamps in a row for a festival.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern lets us say what comes next without looking.

warmup.q: What do we call a thing that makes its own light?
Is a steel spoon a light source?
warmup.a: No. It only shines when light falls on it.

warmup.q: Name a light source that is alive.
What does a diya need to keep burning?
What happens when you switch off a torch in the dark?

roots.context: We have tested which things shine in the dark, and switched a torch on and off. Now we ask what that tells us about light, about ourselves and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the dark room, the torch lit things only while it was switched on. The dark came back the moment it went off. So the torch makes new light every moment. Every lamp needs oil, cells or electricity to keep making it.
deep_truth.habit: We talk about light as if it fills a room and stays there, like water in a tank. The torch test shows a room has light only while a light source keeps making it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the dark room test, the dark came back the instant the torch went off. When a grown-up blew out the diya, its light was gone at once too.

three.who_am_i: You are someone who sees by light. Every time you see a face you love, light from a light source has bounced off that face into your eyes.
three.what_is_life: Almost all life on Earth runs on the Sun's light. Plants catch sunlight to make food, and humans and other animals eat the plants.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of light sources, from the Sun and the stars to flames, lamps and fireflies. Each one keeps making new light while it shines.

roots.thread: Sesame and coconut plants catch sunlight and store some of that energy in oil. When the oil burns in a diya, that energy comes out again as light and heat. So the light of a diya began as sunlight, caught by a plant. Everything is aware in its own way, the Sun and a flame too. Many scientists disagree: they say only living beings with nerves are aware.

teachings.teaching: The Sun is new each day.
teachings.link: Like the torch in the dark room, the Sun keeps making new light. The sunlight on your face this morning left the Sun only about 8 minutes before, not yesterday.

teachings.teaching: Lead me from darkness to light.
teachings.link: In the dark room, a light source led you from darkness to light. You could see your hand only when the torch was making light.

science.text: A light source makes its own light. Its light travels away from it all the time, and when it stops making light, the light stops coming.
The Sun's light and heat come from hydrogen joining to make helium, deep inside the Sun.

other_view.view: They say a lamp, a flame and the Sun are not aware of anything. To them, a flame is only oil and air changing into new things, and a torch is only electricity passing through a tiny lamp. They think awareness belongs to living beings with nerves or brains.

practice.title: The glowing spot behind your eyes
practice.say: A grown-up lights a diya and puts it on a plate, an arm's length away. Sit still and look gently at the flame. Count slowly to ten. Now close your eyes. Can you still see a glowing spot? Watch it fade slowly. When it is gone, open your eyes. If you have no diya, sit by a sunny window with your eyes closed and feel the warm light on your eyelids. Never look at the Sun itself.
practice.kid: Look gently at the flame. Count to ten. Now close your eyes. Can you see a glowing spot? Watch it fade.

ask: When you closed your eyes, the spot glowed for a while. Was that light in the room, or in you?
The torch makes new light every moment. Are you new every moment too?
If the Sun is a light source and you see by the Sun, where does your seeing start?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged with eyes closed, a diya on a plate in front, and a soft glowing spot drawn above the child's head as what the child sees with eyes closed.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many astronomers thought the Sun was made of much the same stuff as the Earth: rock and metals like iron. In the 1920s, a young woman called Cecilia Payne studied the light of the Sun and other stars. She was from England, but her university there did not give women full degrees, so she went to study in America. She used a rule worked out a few years earlier by Meghnad Saha, a scientist from Bengal in India. His rule showed how a star's heat changes its light. With it, she could work out what each star is made of. In 1925 she found that stars are made mostly of hydrogen, the lightest gas, with helium next. A famous astronomer, Henry Norris Russell, told her this was impossible. So she wrote that her result was probably not real. Four years later, Russell's own work showed that she had been right. Today we know the Sun is a huge ball of very hot gas, mostly hydrogen. Deep inside it, hydrogen joins to make helium, and that makes the Sun's light and heat.
how_we_found_out.who: Cecilia Payne, an English-American astronomer; Meghnad Saha, an Indian scientist from Bengal; Henry Norris Russell, an American astronomer
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Astronomers thought the Sun and stars were made of much the same stuff as the Earth. Cecilia Payne showed from their light that they are mostly hydrogen, and four years later other astronomers agreed.

founder: ideas/by_topic/light-seeing-and-shadows.md: the founder's trataka (steady candle-gazing) idea became the Roots practice, done briefly with a diya at arm's length and with a sunny window instead for families without a flame. Her 'flash-light chase' and 'photon tag' physical games grew into Torch On, Torch Off. Her note on fireflies lighting the night became the firefly cards, spotted card and video. Her deeper ideas (photons, speed of light, the 8-minute trip, glow sticks and the dark box) belong to the Level 3 light units, so this unit does not repeat them.

Curriculum entry sci.light.light-sources.L1 (Sun, lamp, fire, torch: things that give light). No board chapter is listed for this level. The Level 2 unit goes on to the Moon and to darkness as the absence of light, so this unit only prepares for those ideas.
science: Cecilia Payne, Stellar Atmospheres (PhD thesis, Radcliffe College, 1925): stars are mostly hydrogen and helium. H. N. Russell, 'On the composition of the Sun's atmosphere', Astrophysical Journal 70 (1929), confirmed it.
M. N. Saha, 'Ionization in the solar chromosphere', Philosophical Magazine 40 (1920): the ionisation equation Payne used.
The Nobel Prize in Physics 2014, to Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura, for efficient blue light-emitting diodes, which made bright, energy-saving white light sources possible.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach the Earth (about 150 million km at about 300,000 km per second). The Sun's volume is about 1.3 million times the Earth's.

Kobayashi, Kikuchi and Okamura, 'Imaging of ultraweak spontaneous photon emission from human body displaying diurnal rhythm', PLoS ONE 4 (2009): the human body gives off light about 1,000 times weaker than the eye can see.
Fireflies (beetles of the family Lampyridae) make light by a chemical reaction in their abdomen and use flash patterns to find mates.
Heraclitus, fragment DK 22 B6, quoted by Aristotle, Meteorology 355a13: 'The sun is new each day.' Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.3.28: 'tamaso ma jyotir gamaya', lead me from darkness to light.

playtest: Walked through the dark room test, the far-wall test, the three activities, the star lantern, the power-cut challenge and both games as a parent and a 6-year-old would in a flat. Cut the dark room test to 15 minutes by taking out its diya extra (the diya has its own activity), and fixed the cards, answers and evidence that mentioned it. Made the card sorting game playable: cards stay on their paper, wrong ones turn face down, and the count and the NOT NOW question use those. Gave the moving game a score for one child and a new check, so torch-off is not asked again. Introduced Nisha in the mirror check.
